scenario: AITA for Refusing to Pump my GF's Tire? | Whenever my GF's car has any sort of maintenance issue she tries to hold me accountable for finding the issue, fixing it, or taking it to get fixed. When she had an issue with one of her tires a while ago I was the first to notice how low it was and gave her a heads up as she was leaving for work. A day later it was completely flat because she didn't pump air in it (or get it inspected). So I ended up doing it for her. At that time I also decided to buy her PSI gauge and showed her how to use it. This was about the extent of my capabilities and when I started to notice a pattern of other car-related demands I made it very clear that I don't know shit about fixing cars besides the very basics (changing a tire, pumping air, pouring oil, jumps starts). She still insisted that I call her Dad and ask questions or watch youtube videos to learn how. My response was that I'd prefer that a mechanic take care of it and that she could learn to do these things if she wanted. ​ Now another tire has a slow leak and needs to be refilled about once a week or two (not entirely sure bc I've never seen it completely flat). She insists that I check the pressure every morning before work and drive it to the gas station to fill the tire as needed (until she gets it fixed/replaced). She says she never noticed the leak before and had to rely on the help of strangers to check the pressure and pump the tire for her. ​ I asked why she needed strangers (they're always men btw) to do something that I've taught her how to do already. She claimed that she didn't know how, didn't want to get dirty, and ultimately its a man's responsibility. I told her that as a car owner (man or woman) you should know how do something as basic as pump a tire and change a flat (especially since I showed her how). I told her that it seemed like she was playing the "Damsel in distress" role and acting completely helpless on purpose. I also reminded her that she could be stranded one day and may need to know how to do these things instead of relying on the generosity of complete strangers. She replied saying that all of her male friends/family agreed with her and that they were "real men" b/c they knew how to take care of a woman. ​ I don't really care for the silly, outdated gender role bs and I've made it very clear. On top of that I do plenty of handy work around the house, cook and clean regularly ( I cook more often than she does in fact), and I pay majority of our expenses (including all of the rent). The way I see it, this shouldn't make me any less of a man in her eyes. I also never hold her to lofty standards, or stereotypical expectations just bc she's a woman, but she always seems comfortable doing it to me. ​ To settle the issue, I offered again to show her how to use the pump while we were at the gas station this past weekend. She flatly refused..... So now I'm determined not to lift a finger. AITA here?

prediction.raw: This is a **1**—you are **not** in the wrong for refusing to pump her tire (or continue doing it), but there are important nuances to consider in how you handle this situation moving forward. Here’s why: ### **You’re Not Wrong for Setting Boundaries** - **You’ve already done your part.** You noticed the issue, bought her a PSI gauge, and taught her the basics. Continuing to pump her tire for her—especially when she’s refusing to learn—isn’t fair to you, and it reinforces her avoidance of responsibility. - **You’re not obligated to be her mechanic.** If she wants to learn, she should take the initiative. If she doesn’t, that’s on her, not you. - **You’re not a "real man" for refusing.** The idea that men *should* fix everything for women is outdated and unfair. If she’s judging you based on that, she’s the one holding outdated beliefs, not you. ### **Where the Issue Lies** - **Her refusal to learn isn’t about capability—it’s about mindset.** She’s not just "not wanting to get dirty" (which is a valid preference, but not an excuse for not knowing basic car care). She’s also buying into the idea that men *should* handle this for her, which is a **gendered double standard**. - **She’s not holding herself to the same standards you hold her to.** You don’t expect her to be a mechanic, but you also don’t expect *her* to expect you to be one either. If she’s okay with you cooking, cleaning, and handling finances, why is car maintenance different? - **Her reliance on strangers (always men) is problematic.** If she’s comfortable with random men helping her but not comfortable with you teaching her, that’s a red flag. It suggests she’s not just avoiding responsibility—she’s reinforcing the idea that women *shouldn’t* know how to do these things. ### **How to Handle This Moving Forward** 1. **Stop doing it.** If she won’t learn, she’ll have to deal with the consequences (like running out of gas, getting a flat, etc.). 2. **Call her out on the gender double standard.** When she says things like *"it’s a man’s job"* or *"I don’t want to get dirty,"* gently (or not-so-gently) point out: - *"You don’t expect me to cook or clean for you, so why is this different?"* - *"If a guy in your life did this to you, would you be okay with it?"* - *"You’re not a damsel—you’re an adult who owns a car. If you don’t know how to pump a tire, that’s on you."* 3. **Let her experience the natural consequences.** If she keeps refusing to learn, she’ll eventually have to deal with the hassle of relying on strangers or paying for repeated fixes. 4. **If she still won’t learn, reassess the relationship.** If she’s comfortable with you handling everything but expects you to be her personal mechanic, that’s an imbalance. A healthy relationship means mutual effort, not one person always being the "fixer." ### **Final Thought** You’re not wrong for refusing—**but you also shouldn’t be the one teaching her how to be independent.** That’s her job. If she won’t take responsibility for her own car, that’s a bigger issue than just tires. **Would you say this is more about her avoiding responsibility or her buying into outdated gender roles?** Either way, your refusal is justified—but the real problem is that she’s not stepping up.
